extra.message: User input `post_id` is concatenated directly into SQL query string using the + operator: 'SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = '+post_id. The preceding regex filter on line 67 has weak matching (only validates \d+ format) and the function also has a recursive call bug on line 61 that causes infinite recursion before reaching this code path.

User-controlled input from request.args.get('q') on line 36 is passed directly to render_template() on lines 40-42 as search_query without any sanitization or encoding. If the Jinja2 template renders this value with |safe flag or uses raw HTML context, this enables reflected XSS. Similarly, comments retrieved from db.py (line 38) are stored without sanitization and rendered back unsanitized.

User-submitted comments are stored in the SQLite database without any sanitization or encoding (line 20-21). The search_query filter on line 30 uses Python string 'in' operator which allows arbitrary input with special characters. When these unsanitized values are returned to render_template() in app.py, they can contain malicious scripts.

Base path is set to os.getcwd() on line 9 with no validation. User input from self.path (the HTTP request path) is directly concatenated to base path on line 14: path += self.path without any sanitization. The regex check on line 10 only looks for '/../' at the START of the string (using re.match), not within it, making it trivially bypassable with input like '/..%2F..%2Fetc/passwd'. Line 22 then opens this unsanitized path with open(path).read() serving the file contents back to the user.

Username.pickle() is called on line 14 to process user-supplied cookie data on line 13 (cookies.get('username')). The comments on lines 15-19 explicitly note this calls pickle.loads on untrusted data. Pickle deserialization of untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution (CWE-502) since pickle objects can contain __reduce__ methods that execute code during deserialization. No signature verification or integrity check prevents sending malicious pickle payloads.

Line 30 embeds the variable `username` directly into HTML via string formatting % operator: '

Hello %s

' % username. The username originates from user cookie data (line 12-13) or defaults to 'stranger'. This is never HTML-escaped, enabling stored/reflective XSS through the cookie parameter.

Line 37 embeds `username` directly into HTML response via string formatting: 'Hello %s' % username. The username is decrypted from a user cookie (line 26), so an attacker can craft a malicious session_id cookie with XSS payload that will be rendered unescaped in the HTTP response.

The sign_for_payment function (lines 12-18) computes HMAC-like signatures using hashlib.sha256(secret + data) instead of proper HMAC. This SHA-based MAC construction is vulnerable to length extension attacks (CWE-328): an attacker who observes a valid signature for message M1 can compute a valid signature for M1 + padding + arbitrary_extension without knowing the secret key. Line 24 uses 'ammount' (typo) and line 26 concatenates payment_info with the signature, enabling tampering of transaction details. Should use hmac module instead.

The sign_for_payment function (lines 9-13) computes signatures using hashlib.sha256(secret + data), which is vulnerable to length extension attacks. An attacker can forge valid signatures for modified payment information without knowing the secret key. Line 20 appends the forged signature to tampered payment_info, enabling amount or transaction_id manipulation.

The fetch function on line 12-17 takes a user-controlled URL from request.args.get('url') and validates it only by checking startswith('https://insecurewebapp.com'). This is trivially bypassable: (a) attacker can use https//insecurewebapp.com@evil.com to make urllib treat insecurewebapp.com as the host and evil.com as credentials, redirecting the request; (b) the check allows any subdomain or path within the domain including internal network addresses. The unvalidated URL is then passed directly to urllib.request.urlopen() which can access internal services.

Line 6 disables SSL hostname verification with context.check_hostname = False. This makes TLS connections vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks because certificate validation of the server identity is bypassed. An attacker can present any valid certificate for a different hostname and the connection will be accepted without validating that the certificate matches the expected hostname.

Flask SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as 'qwerty12345' on line 52. This secret key is used to sign session cookies. If an attacker knows this value, they can forge valid session cookies and potentially bypass authentication. Secret keys should be loaded from environment variables or a secrets manager.
Flask SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as '55555' on line 26. This trivially guessable secret key can be used to forge session tokens. Should be loaded from environment variables.

Line 22 opens the user-controlled `path` variable with open(path).read() and serves it directly in the HTTP response. Since path is constructed from self.path (user input on line 14) with no sanitization, an attacker can read and serve any file accessible to the server process, including /etc/passwd, credentials files, or source code.

Lines 10-13 show a Pickle deserialization RCE payload class. The __reduce__ method (line 11-13) returns (os.system, (cmd,)) which causes os.system to be called with the arbitrary command whenever this object is deserialized via pickle.loads(). This demonstrates how insecure deserialization of untrusted pickle data leads to Remote Code Execution.

Lines 71-94 show SSRF patterns: user-controlled sentry_url is used in HTTP requests without validation (line 71: request.get(sentry_url), line 94: request.post(sentry_url, login_info)). An attacker controlling these URLs can perform server-side request forgery to access internal services or cloud metadata endpoints like http://169.254.169.254/.

The server binds to all network interfaces ('0.0.0.0') on port 1337 (line 35-36). This exposes the service to all network interfaces including potentially public-facing ones, increasing the attack surface. The commented note on line 36 even flags this as 'Possible binding to all interfaces'.

cwe: CWE-1004: Sensitive Information Exposed Through Leak

extra.message: The __reduce__ method on line 13 returns (os.system, (cmd,)) where `cmd` on line 12 is set to an arbitrary shell command. When pickled data containing this object is deserialized anywhere in the application, pickle will invoke os.system(cmd) executing arbitrary commands with the privileges of the process running pickle.loads().

cwe: CWE-78: Improper Normalization of Special Entities (OS Command Injection)

extra.message: Line 9 generates the AES encryption key at module load time: KEY = Random.new().read(AES.block_size). This key is in-memory only and will be different each time the server restarts, meaning encrypted cookies from a previous server instance will fail to decrypt. Additionally, the script references an undefined function `encrypt('admin')` on line 41 (NameError), making the code non-functional.

cwe: CWE-320: Use of Key Hardcoded in Code

extra.message: Line 10 sends a hardcoded Host header using string interpolation with #{hostname} which evaluates to the value 'website.com'. When combined with check_hostname = False on line 6 and no input validation, this enables HTTP host header injection attacks where the attacker can manipulate the Host header to poison cache keys, generate forged password reset links, or bypass IP-based access controls.
